attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b2244235
attributes.field_kotobagaki: あふさかにて人をわかれける時によめる
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: あふさかにて人をわかれける時によめる
attributes.field_text: 相坂の/ 関しまさしき / 物ならは / あかすわかるる / 君をととめよ
attributes.field_text_romaji: Ausaka no / sekishi masashiki / mono naraba / akazu wakaruru / kimi o todome yo
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Ausaka no / sekishi masashiki / mono naraba / akazu wakaruru / kimi o todome yo
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'oh barrier of / Ōsaka \tif restraint/ indeed you are \thold/ back that one who wishes to/ leave before farewells are done', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.154'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b2244236
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 藤原のこれをかかむさしのすけにまかりける時に、をくりにあふさかをこゆとてよみける
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 藤原のこれをかかむさしのすけにまかりける時に、をくりにあふさかをこゆとてよみける
attributes.field_text: かつこえて / 別れもゆくか / 相坂は / 人たのめなる / なにこそ有けれ
attributes.field_text_romaji: Katsu koete / wakare mo yuku ka / Ausaka wa / hitodanome naru / na ni koso arikere
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Katsu koete / wakare mo yuku ka / Ausaka wa / hitodanome naru / na ni koso arikere
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'while still he crosses/ over and journeys onward/ leaving me behind/ your title \tŌsaka/ Meeting Hill \tis just a name', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.159'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b2244237
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 題知らず
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 題知らず
attributes.field_text: 音羽山/ をとにききつつ / 相坂の / 関のこなたに / 年をふる哉
attributes.field_text_romaji: Otowayama / oto ni kikitsutsu / Ausaka no / seki no konata ni / toshi o furu kana
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Otowayama / oto ni kikitsutsu / Ausaka no / seki no konata ni / toshi o furu kana
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'I hear rumors of/ her \tborne by Mount Sound of Wings/ and yet here on the/  far side of Meeting Hill I/ pass the years in barren dreams', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.184'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b2244238
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 題知らず
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 題知らず
attributes.field_text: 逢坂の / ゆふつけ鳥も / 我ことく / 人や恋しき / ねのみ鳴らん
attributes.field_text_romaji: Ausaka no / yūtsugedori mo / waga gotoku / hitoya koishiki / ne nomi nakuran
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Ausaka no / yūtsugedori mo / waga gotoku / hitoya koishiki / ne nomi nakuran
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'does the beribboned/ cock of Meeting Hill share my/ unfulfilled longings  ̶ / is it for love alone that/ we raise our solemn voices', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.202'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b2244239
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 題知らず
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 題知らず
attributes.field_text: あふさかの / 関になかるる / いはし水 / いはて心に / おもひこそすれ
attributes.field_text_romaji: Ausaka no / seki ni nagaruru / iwashimizu / iwa de kokoro ni / omoi koso sure
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Ausaka no / seki ni nagaruru / iwashimizu / iwa de kokoro ni / omoi koso sure
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'the fresh spring waters/ surge freely through the rocky/ crevices of the/ Barrier at Meeting Hill \tbut/ My words of love remain checked', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.203'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b224423a
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 題知らず
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 題知らず
attributes.field_text: 恋恋て / 稀にこよひそ / 逢坂の / 夕つけ鳥は / なかすもあら南
attributes.field_text_romaji: Koi koi te / mare ni koyoi zo / Ausaka no / yūtsugedori wa / nakazu mo aranan
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Koi koi te / mare ni koyoi zo / Ausaka no / yūtsugedori wa / nakazu mo aranan
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'I have yearned so long/ and at last tonight we meet  ̶ / may the beribboned/ cock at Ōsaka never/ announce the break of day', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.231'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b224423b
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 中納言源ののほるの朝臣のあふみのすけに侍ける時に、よみてやれりける
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 中納言源ののほるの朝臣のあふみのすけに侍ける時に、よみてやれりける
attributes.field_text: 相坂の / 夕つけとりに / あらはこそ / 君かゆききを / なくなくも見め
attributes.field_text_romaji: Ausaka no / yūtsugedori ni / araba koso / kimi ga yukiki o / nakunaku mo mime
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Ausaka no / yūtsugedori ni / araba koso / kimi ga yukiki o / nakunaku mo mime
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'oh if I could be/ the beribboned cock of the/ Ōsaka Road \thow/ plaintively I would cry out/ as I watched you come and go', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.261-262'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b224423c
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 題知らず
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 題知らず
attributes.field_text: 逢坂の / 嵐のかせは / さむけれと / 行ゑしらねは / 侘つつそぬる
attributes.field_text_romaji: Ausaka no / arashi no kaze wa / samukeredo / yukue shiraneba / wabitsutsu zo nuru
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Ausaka no / arashi no kaze wa / samukeredo / yukue shiraneba / wabitsutsu zo nuru
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'in Ōsaka/ the howling tempests rage and/  winds lash cold \tbut still/ I know no place to go \tso/  I’ll sleep here in misery', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.333'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b224423d
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 奥山菅の根しのきふる雪下
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 奥山菅の根しのきふる雪下
attributes.field_text: ＊わきもこす / あふさか山の / しのすすき / ほには出すも / 恋わたる哉/＊１わきもこかイ/＊１わきもこにイ
attributes.field_text_romaji: Wagimo kosu / Ausaka yama no / shinosusuki / ho ni wa idezu mo / koi wataru kana
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Wagimo kosu / Ausaka yama no / shinosusuki / ho ni wa idezu mo / koi wataru kana
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': 'my passion shall stay/ hidden as the unopened/ buds of plume grasses/  on the Ōsaka slopes/ where I met my beloved', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.376-377'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b224423e
attributes.field_text: 夏草を見て、妻を恋ひ、逢坂山に至りて、手向けを祈り、
attributes.field_text_romaji: natsukusa o mite, tsuma o koi, Ausaka yama ni itarite, tamuke o inori,…
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: natsukusa o mite, tsuma o koi, Ausaka yama ni itarite, tamuke o inori,…
attributes.field_translations: [{'text': '[…] on yearning for one’s wife when one sees […] the grasses of summer, on offering prayer stripes on Ōsaka Hill, […]', 'source': 'Rodd, Laurel R. and Henkenius, Mary C. (1984): p.47'}]

attributes.title: 5bfc17e2a7372ae5b224423f

attributes.field_kotobagaki: 返し
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 返し

attributes.field_text_romaji_long: sekimori wa / aratamaru chō / Ausaka no / yūtsugedori wa / nakitsutsu zo yuku

attributes.field_kotobagaki: あひにける女の、またあはさりけれは

attributes.field_text_romaji_long: shirazarishi / toki dani koeshi / Ausaka o / nado ima sara ni / ware madouran

attributes.title: 5bfc17e3a7372ae5b2244243
attributes.field_kotobagaki: 題知らず
attributes.field_kotobagaki_long: 題知らず
attributes.field_text: 思ひやる / 心はつねに / かよへとも / あふ坂の関 / こえすもあるかな
attributes.field_text_romaji: omoiyaru / kokoro wa tsune ni / kayoedomo / Ausaka no seki / koezu mo aru kana
attributes.field_text_romaji_long: omoiyaru / kokoro wa tsune ni / kayoedomo / Ausaka no seki / koezu mo aru kana

attributes.field_text_romaji_long: chikakereba / nanika wa shirushi / Ausaka no / sekino soto zoto / omoitaenan

attributes.field_text_romaji_long: Ausaka no / seki tomeraruru / ware nareba / afumi (ōmi) chōran / kata mo shirarezu

attributes.field_text_romaji_long: yukikaeri / kite mo kikanan / Ausaka no / seki ni kawareru / hito mo ari ya to

attributes.field_kotobagaki: 女につかはしける

attributes.field_text: 夜もすから / ＊ぬれてわひつる / から衣 / あふ坂山に / 道まとひして / ＊２ぬれてわひつつイ

玉もにあそぶをしのこゑこゑなど、哀に聞えて、しめしめと人めすくなき、宮のうちの有様に、「さも、うつり行世かれ」と、おぼしつづくるに、へいぢうがまねならねど、まことに、涙もろになん。昔にかわりて、おとなおとなしくは聞え給ものから、「これを、かくてや」と、ひきうごかし給ふ。

　　年月を中に隔て逢坂のさもせきがたくおつるなみだか

女、

　　涙のみせきとめがたきし水にて行あふ道ははやく絶にき

など、かけはなれ聞え給へど、いにしへをおぼし出づるも、「たれにより、おほうは、さるいみじきこともありし、世のさはぎぞ」と、思ひ出給ふに、「げに、今一たびの對面は、ありもすべかりけり」と、おぼしよはるも、もとより、づしやかなる所はおはせざりし人の、とし頃は、さまさまに、世中を思ひしり、きしかたを、くやしく、おほやけ・わたくしのことにふれつつ、数もなくおぼしあつめて、いといたく、過し給にたれど、昔おぼえたる御對面に、其世のことも、とをからぬ心ちして、え心づよくも、もてなし給はず。

attributes.title: 6032780ad063ad58294a6534
attributes.field_text: 今は、まして、いとはづかしう、よろづのこと、うひうひしき心ちすれど、めつらしきにや、えしのばれざりけむ、「あふさかの関やいかなるせきなればしけき嘆のなかをわくらん。夢のやうになん」ときこえたり。「あはれもつらさも、わすれぬふし」と、おぼしをかれたる人なれば、をりをりは、なを、のたまひうごかしけり。かかるほとに、このひたちのかみ、いのつもりにや、なやまうのみして、物こころぼそかりければ、子どもに、ただ、この君の御ことをのみ、いひをきて、「よろづのこと、ただこの御こころにのみまかせて、わがありつる世にかはらで、つかうまつれ」とのみ、明くれ、いひけり。

ふりすててけふは行くともすずか川やそせのなみに袖はぬれじや

ときこえ給へれど、いとくらう、ものさわがしきほどなれば、またの日、せきのあなたよりぞ、御かへしある。

　　すずか河八十瀬のなみにぬれぬれずいせまでたれか思ひをこせむ

ことそぎてかき給へるしも、御て、いと、よしよししく、なまめきたるに、「あはれなるけを、すこしそへ給へらましかば」とおぼす。霧いたう降りて、ただならぬあさけに、うちながめて、ひとりごちおはす。

　　行かたをながめもやらん此秋はあふ坂山をきりなへだてそ

にしのたいにもわたり給はで、ひとやりならず、物さびしげに、ながめくらし給ふ。まして、たびのそらは、いかに御心づくしなることおほかりけん。

attributes.title: 60ad0002ff67c34b74956641
attributes.field_text:
昔、男有けり。その男、伊勢の國にかりの使にいきけるに、

かの伊勢の齋宮なりける人のおや、「つねの使よりは、此人よくいたはれ」とい

ひやれりければ、親の事なりければ、いとねんごろにいたはりけり。あした

にはかりにいだしたてゝやり、ゆふさりはかへりつゝ、そこにこさせけり。かくてね

ん比にいたづきけり。二日といふ夜、男、われて「あはん｣といふ。女

もはたいとあはじとも思へらず。されど、人めしげゝれば、えあはず。つかひざね

とある人なれば、遠くもやとさず。女のねやもちかく有ければ、女、人をしづめ

て、ねひとつばかりに、男のもとにきたりけり。男はたねられざりければ、とのかたを見いたしてふせるに、月のおぼろなるに、ちひさきわらはをさきにたて

ゝ、人立てり。男、いとうれしくて、わがねる所にゐて入て、ねひとつ

よりうし三つまであるに、まだ何事もかたらはぬにかへりにけり。男、いとか

なしくて、ねず成にけり。つとめて、いぶかしけれど、わが人をやるべきに

しあらねば、いと心もとなくて待ちをれば、あけはなれてしばしあるに、女の

許より、詞はなくて、

　　君やこし我や行けんおもほえず夢かうつゝかねてかさめてか

　男、いといたうなきてよめる。

　　かきくらす心のやみにまどひにき夢うつゝとは今夜さだめよ

とよみてやりて、かりに出ぬ。野にありけど、心はそらにて、こよひだに人しつ

めて、いとゝくあはんと思ふに、國のかみ、いつきの宮のかみかけたる、かりの使

有と聞て、夜ひとよさけのみしければ、もはらあひこともえせで、あけはおは

りの國へたちなんとすれば、男も人しれずちの泪をながせど、えあはず。夜や

う＋＋あけなんとする程に、女かたよりいだすさかづきのさらに、歌を書て出し

たり。とりて見れば、

　　かち人のわたれどぬれぬえにしあれば

とかきて、すゑはなし。その盃のさらに、ついまつのすみして、歌のすゑをかきつく。

　　またあふさかのせきはこえなん

とて、明くれはおはりの國へこえにけり。

　齋宮は水の尾の御時、文徳天皇の御むすめ、これたかのいもうと。

It means that the gate of the Ōsaka barrier, which protects Kyōto from the barbarians of the eastern provinces, is not closed. In other words, it signifies that the world is peaceful due to righteous governance.

field_commentary_eng.value: Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, in his campaign to quell the eastern barbarians, declares, "Under heaven, which place in the land of the Emperor would be no royal territory?" Since ancient times, this bridge has been a strategic point in the defense against enemies from the eastern provinces. With ease, Tamuramaro crosses this bridge, further illustrating his courage as he heads eastward.

field_commentary_eng.value:
Sekidera Komachi is a Nō play that portrays the elderly Ono no Komachi living near the Ōsaka barrier. The Komachi depicted here is sometimes portrayed as reclusive and cynically detached. The word "Ōsaka (written Ausaka)" serves as a pivot word, evoking "meeting (au) the Buddhist teachings." The line, "The mountain wind at Ōsaka. If only I could truly grasp the principle of 'all conditioned phenomena being transient,'" reflects her self-deprecating acknowledgment. While living at Ōsaka barrier, she ought to have embraced the Buddhist truth of shōmetsuhō ("all things that are born must eventually perish"), yet she admits she cannot fully internalize such profound teachings. This suggests the old woman’s nihilistic belief that human beings cannot completely attain enlightenment.
The old woman also expresses that, "In the moments of falling blossoms and scattering leaves," she continues to engage in "the beloved path," referring to the art of waka poetry, even as she declines into old age.

field_commentary_eng.value:
At the eastern edge of the capital, on mount Ōsaka, a decree is issued to abandon Prince Semimaru—a figure considered ominous to the Emperor. The retainers obediently carry out this decision. Prince Semimaru, exiled by his father to the remote region of Mount Ōsaka, experiences profound despair and anxiety, captured through the imagery of "twisting a single thread" (kataito o yoru), which leads to the expression (yorube nashi) being "without support or refuge". This metaphor not only conveys his isolation but also evokes the idea of "twisting threads together," symbolizing the concept of "meeting" (au), which ties into the significance of the barrier Ōsaka (Ōsaka no seki).
The analogy of the blind turtle and floating log is also invoked to deepen this expression. It refers to the nearly impossible chance of a blind turtle in the vast ocean encountering a piece of wood with a hole that perfectly fits its neck. This metaphor, rooted in Buddhist teachings, illustrates how rare and precious it is for a person to encounter Buddha’s teachings in this world. Semimaru’s blindness reflects his uncertain state, and his doubts about whether he can truly encounter and embrace Buddhist teachings while living in exile at Mount Ōsaka mirror this existential uncertainty.

field_commentary_eng.value:
"The staff Henjō composed a poem about" refers to the following waka:
"The awe-inspiring gods must have carved it? If you lean on this staff you will surely reach the steep slope of a thousand years (of age)." (Kokin wakashū 348).
This poem was written on the occasion when Emperor Kōkō, while still a prince, presented his eighty-year-old aunt with a silver staff in celebration of her long life. The phrase "tsuku kara ni" cleverly plays on the dual meanings of "to lean on a staff" and "to be possessed by a deity" (kami ga tsuku).
While the staff in Henjō's poem symbolizes "a thousand years of prosperity," in the context of Mount Ōsaka, it becomes a poignant expression for the support in a humble straw hut. The unjust and painful reality of Semimaru's life is expressed through the phrase, "In such a sorrowful world, at Ōsaka" (kakaru ukiyo ni Ōsaka no), which reflects his plight. This reference to mount Ōsaka is then connected to Semimaru’s famous waka:
"Here it is: the gate / where people coming and going / must part company, / where both friends and strangers meet ̶ / on the slopes of Meeting Hill" (Gosen wakashū 1089, transl. Steven Carter).
Drawing on this, the phrase, “Whether known or unknown, behold this!” (shiru mo shiranu mo kore miyo ya) follows.
The notion of Semimaru being an "imperial prince of the Engi era" (i.e., a son of Emperor Daigo) stems from a passage in "The Tale of the Heike" (Heike Monogatari, Kakuichibon text), in the section "Volume 10: The Journey Down the Eastern Sea Road."

Semimaru’s sister, the imperial princess Sakagami (Reversed Hair), appears as a crazed woman with disheveled, upstanding hair, yet it is sung that her heart is pure. This connects to "seki no shimizu" ("the pure water of the barrier").
The poem,
"On the surface of the pure water of Ōsaka Barrier, a reflection appears —Now at full moon must they be passing with the horses (from Shinano to the capital)" (Shūi wakashū, 170), is attributed to Ki no Tsurayuki.
The phrase "reflection appears" is a poetic association (engo, linked word) with "full moon" (mochizuki). Additionally, "mochizuki" refers to a place name in Shinano province (modern-day Nagano prefecture), from which horses were offered to the imperial court. This evokes an image of crossing Mount Ōsaka in search of horses on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival (the fifteenth night of the eighth lunar month).

The phrase "kakaru kitoku ni Ōsaka no" ("such a wondrous blessing at Ōsaka") conveys the joy of receiving the grace of the Sumiyoshi deity. This joy is linked to "seki no shimizu ni" ("the pure water of the barrier"), calling to mind Tsurayuki's waka:
"On the surface of the pure water of Ōsaka Barrier, a reflection appears —Now at full moon must they be passing with the horses (from Shinano to the capital)" (Shūi wakashū, 170).
This poem evokes the "horse of the full moon" (mochizuki no koma), a horse either from the Mochizuki region of Shinano province or a pale moon-colored horse, offered to the emperor. The imagery of this horse is introduced at the beginning of the play as the one Tsurayuki had ridden.
The narrative celebrates the miraculous event when this horse, having become unable to move on at the gate of the Aritoshi shrine, was restored to its ability to walk through the divine power of Sumiyoshi Myōjin, the god of poetry. This moment is interpreted as a testament to the power of waka poetry and is sung in praise.

field_commentary_eng.value:
A monk setting out on a pilgrimage to the eastern provinces chants a travel song (michiyuki). Referring to the capital as "karaku" (Flower Capital) in classical Chinese is extremely rare, appearing only three times across the entire Collection of 350 Nō plays. In contrast, the expression "hana no miyako" (blooming capital) is used 49 times, making the former overwhelmingly less common.
In this case, it is thought that the term "karaku" was chosen as it was a word likely used by the monks of the Five Great Temples (Gozan), who were well-versed in Chinese poetry.

field_commentary_eng.value: Crossing the Ōsaka barrier and emerging on the shores of Lake Biwa, one arrives at Matsumoto and Uchidehama. This area is the site of Awazu no seiran ("clear breeze at Awazu"), one of the Eight Views of Ōmi (Ōmi hakkei), which were selected in the early Edo period. The term seiran (clear breeze) describes the wind blowing through pine groves, and it seems that even at the time when nō plays were being written, the area around Matsumoto was associated with the image of a storm. From there, the narrative transitions to Yabase kihan ("Returning sails at Yabase"), another of the Eight Views of Ōmi. Yabase, located on the eastern shore of Lake Biwa, was part of the route for crossing the lake by boat and traveling onward to the eastern provinces (Tōgoku).

field_commentary_eng.value:
"Rokudai gozen" refers to Taira no Takakiyo, the eldest son of Taira no Koremori. Saitō Go and Saitō Roku were brothers and served as Takakiyo's attendants, responsible for looking after him. Similar stories can be found in The Tale of the Heike and The Tale of Rokudai gozen, suggesting that this play may have drawn from one or both of these sources.
"Ōsaka" is a place name along the road from the capital (Kyōto) to Kamakura. In this context, it is used as a poetic pivot to express lament: "How much longer must I wander in this cruel world? Now, at this crossroads of parting from Rokudai, I cross the barrier at Ōsaka and head toward Kamakura." Here, the word "Ōsaka" conveys both the physical journey and an emotional encounter with the fate of possibly parting from Rokudai in death.
